questions: Have you been experiencing involuntary shaking or tremors in your hands?
Do the tremors occur when your hands are at rest?
Do they become worse when you reach for or hold something?
Is one hand affected more than the other?
Do you have weakness or loss of sensation in either arm or hand?
Do you have difficulty walking, problems with balance, or stiffness?
Have you noticed slowness of movement or reduced facial expression?
Do the tremors improve when you are distracted or performing another task?
Have you recently started or changed any medications?
Do you use caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, or recreational drugs regularly?
Does anyone in your family have a similar tremor or a neurological disorder?
Have you had a recent injury, illness, or significant emotional stress?
Have you experienced episodes of confusion, loss of awareness, or seizures?

results: 1. Bedside neurological examination with tremor assessment during rest, posture, action, handwriting, spiral drawing, and object manipulation
cranial nerve examination: normal
mental status / cognitive screen: normal
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
sensory examination (pinprick, vibration, proprioception): burning pain with pronounced touch sensitivity; vibration and proprioception normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): normal
posture and pull test: normal
fundoscopy: normal
tandem gait: normal
Romberg test, repeated with distraction: negative
muscle tone (spasticity, rigidity, paratonia): normal
cerebellar examination (finger-nose, dysdiadochokinesis, nystagmus): normal
finger-tapping for bradykinesia and decrement: no decrement - argues against Parkinson disease
MRC power in all four limbs: 5/5 throughout
sensory examination (including midline splitting, allodynia): burning pain with pronounced sensitivity to touch, fulfilling allodynia criteria
cognitive screen: normal
variability of amplitude, frequency and axis over the examination: irregular, variable frequency around 4-6 Hz, at times combined with myoclonic jerks
observation for excessive slowness or uneconomic posture: no bradykinesia, no parkinsonian features
2. Bedside tremor distractibility and entrainment testing using contralateral rhythmic finger tapping
distractibility testing (complex motor task with the unaffected side): POSITIVE - the tremor decreases or stops when the left arm performs a task such as drinking from a cup
entrainment testing (tap to an externally paced rhythm): POSITIVE - amplitude falls and the rhythm becomes irregular under repetitive voluntary movement of the other side

surface EMG tremor analysis with accelerometry (frequency, coherence): no abnormality of the kind seen in organic tremor
